title: “AS MOSES LIFTED UP THE SERPENT…” — THE TERRIFYING OLD TESTAMENT STORY JESUS HID IN PLAIN SIGHT BEFORE JOHN 3:16
paragraphs: “AS MOSES LIFTED UP THE SERPENT…” — THE TERRIFYING OLD TESTAMENT STORY JESUS HID IN PLAIN SIGHT BEFORE JOHN 3:16

Before Jesus spoke the most beloved words in Christianity, He pointed to a wilderness filled with dying sinners, poisonous serpents, and a bronze serpent hanging on a pole. What happened there reveals something about the Cross that many believers have read past their entire lives. And once you see the connection, you may never read “For God so loved the world” the same way again.
There is something deeply unsettling about the fact that one of the most beautiful promises in the entire Bible was introduced through one of the strangest stories in the Old Testament.
Not through a wedding.
Not through a beautiful sunrise.
Not through a mother holding her newborn child.
But through snakes.
Venom.
Rebellion.
People dying in the wilderness.
And a bronze serpent lifted high enough for the dying to see.
Why would Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, choose that story to explain what He came to do?
Why would the Savior of the world compare His coming crucifixion to an image of the very creature associated with deception and humanity's fall?
And why did He bring it up while speaking to Nicodemus, a respected religious teacher who probably knew more Scripture than most people around him?
There is a reason.
And it is more personal than you might think.
Because somewhere between the poisoned Israelites in the wilderness and the religious man standing before Jesus in the darkness, we discover a truth that reaches into our own secret battles.
The things we hide.
The sins we excuse.
The prayers we keep postponing.
The spiritual wounds we pretend are not killing us.
And the Savior who came not merely to make wounded people feel better, but to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
To understand John 3:16, we need to listen carefully to what Jesus said immediately before it.
And to understand that, we must travel backward.
Far backward.
To a wilderness where an entire generation was learning what happens when the human heart begins to despise the very mercy keeping it alive.
The story begins in Numbers 21.
Israel had already witnessed miracles that should have been impossible to forget.
God had delivered them from Egyptian slavery. He had opened the sea before them. He had provided water in the wilderness and manna from heaven.
They had seen enough to know that their God was faithful.
Yet suffering has a way of exposing what prosperity can conceal.
The journey became difficult.
The road seemed endless.
The people grew impatient.
And the Bible records something painfully familiar.
“And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?” — Numbers 21:5, KJV
Then came the accusation that revealed the condition of their hearts.
“Our soul loatheth this light bread.”
That bread was God's provision.
The same manna that had sustained them became the very thing they complained about.
Imagine that.
They were being kept alive by mercy, yet they had begun to resent the mercy.
Before we judge them too quickly, perhaps we should remember the last time we complained about a life that God was still sustaining.
The last time we became so consumed with what we lacked that we forgot what we had been spared.
The last time we prayed for deliverance, received an answer, and eventually began treating the blessing as ordinary.
Sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not open rebellion that shocks everyone.
Sometimes it is a heart that has grown accustomed to grace.
A heart that still knows religious language but has lost its gratitude.
A heart that remembers what God has done but no longer trusts Him with what comes next.
And in that wilderness, rebellion met judgment.
Numbers 21:6 says:
“And the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.” — KJV
The Hebrew expression is הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים (hanneḥashim hasseraphim), referring to the burning or fiery serpents.
The description likely evokes the burning pain associated with their bites. The passage does not require us to imagine supernatural, flame-breathing snakes. Its horror is already sufficient.
Real bites.
Real suffering.
Real death.
And suddenly, the people who had complained about their journey were confronted with the possibility that they might never finish it.
Can you picture the scene?
A father clutching his wounded arm.
A mother desperately holding a child.
People looking around and realizing that the danger was not merely uncomfortable.
It was deadly.
Their rebellion was no longer something they could dismiss as harmless frustration.
And then something changed.
The people came to Moses.
“We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD, and against thee; pray unto the LORD, that he take away the serpents from us.” — Numbers 21:7, KJV
Three words should stop us.
We have sinned.
Not, “We were misunderstood.”
Not, “The circumstances made us do it.”
Not, “Everyone else was complaining too.”
We have sinned.
There is a kind of honesty that begins only when our excuses finally run out.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because many of us want God to remove the consequences of our decisions while we continue defending the decisions themselves.
We want relief without repentance.
Peace without surrender.
Forgiveness without admitting what needs forgiving.
We want Jesus to heal what hurts while keeping Him away from what we refuse to release.
But the people in the wilderness finally confessed.
Moses prayed for them.
And God's answer was astonishing.
He did not immediately remove every serpent.
Instead, He gave Moses an instruction.
“Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.” — Numbers 21:8, KJV
Read that again.
God did not command the people to develop an antidote.
He did not tell the strongest Israelites to prove themselves worthy.
He did not establish a competition to determine who deserved survival.
He provided a remedy and called the bitten to look.
Numbers 21:9 records that Moses made a serpent of brass, or bronze, and placed it upon a pole.
And those who had been bitten lived when they looked at it.
The bronze itself was not a magical object.
It possessed no independent saving power.
The healing came from God, who graciously appointed the means through which the people would receive His promised deliverance.
And that distinction matters.
Because centuries later, the Israelites began burning incense to that very bronze serpent.
King Hezekiah destroyed it because an object once associated with God's mercy had become an object of idolatrous devotion (2 Kings 18:4).
Think about that.
People can become so attached to the instrument that they forget the God who used it.
We can treasure religious symbols while neglecting the Lord to whom those symbols should point.
We can admire a cross hanging on a wall while resisting the crucified Christ who calls us to repentance.
We can know the vocabulary of salvation and still avoid surrender.
And now the story takes an extraordinary turn.
Centuries after Moses raised that bronze serpent, a man named Nicodemus came to Jesus at night.
He was a Pharisee.
A ruler of the Jews.
A teacher of Israel.
He knew the Scriptures.
He knew the commandments.
He knew the history of his people.
And yet Jesus told him something his religious achievements could never replace.
“Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” — John 3:3, KJV
The Greek expression is γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν (gennēthē anōthen).
The word anōthen can mean “again” or “from above.”
That double meaning matters.
Nicodemus heard the language of another birth and struggled to understand it. Jesus was speaking about the new life that comes from above through the work of the Spirit.
Not religious improvement alone.
Not a more impressive reputation.
Not a polished version of the old self.
A new birth.
And imagine how confronting that must have been for a man who had spent his life studying the things of God.
He knew the Law, but he still needed life from above.
He possessed religious standing, but he still needed the saving work of God.
He could teach others about holiness, but he could not manufacture spiritual rebirth within himself.
Then Jesus reached into the very Scriptures Nicodemus knew.
And He brought him back to the wilderness.
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” — John 3:14–15, KJV
There it is.
The connection.
The bridge between the wilderness and Calvary.
The statement immediately before John 3:16.
In Greek, the opening words are:
Καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ
Kai kathōs Mōysēs hypsōsen ton ophin en tē erēmō.
“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness…”
The verb ὑψόω (hypsoō) means “to lift up” or “to exalt.”
John uses this language in connection with Jesus' death, particularly in John 12:32–33, where the Gospel explicitly explains that Jesus was indicating the kind of death He would die.
The lifting up points to His crucifixion, while John's Gospel also presents the Cross as the place where the glory of Christ is revealed.
But we must understand the comparison correctly.
Jesus was not saying that He was evil like the serpent.
He was not identifying Himself with Satan.
He was not claiming that the bronze image was divine.

The comparison concerns the God-appointed means of rescue: as the dying Israelites were directed to look toward the provision God had raised before them, so sinners must believe in the Son of Man who would be lifted up for their salvation.
There is also a profound difference.
The bronze serpent did not suffer for anyone.
Jesus did.
The bronze serpent could not forgive sin.
Jesus can.
The bronze serpent was an object God used in a particular moment of Israel's history.
Jesus Christ is the living Son of God, the Savior of the world.
And while the Israelites received deliverance from physical death, those who believe in Christ receive eternal life.
This is not a random Old Testament illustration.
It is a carefully chosen revelation of the Gospel.
And it becomes even more breathtaking when we hear what the apostle Paul later wrote.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
Paul is not saying Jesus became morally sinful.
Christ remained sinless.
Rather, the sinless Savior bore our sins in His sacrificial work so that those united to Him might receive righteousness before God.
Galatians 3:13 also declares that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, pointing to the shameful death of one hung upon a tree.
Now look again at the wilderness.
A deadly affliction.
A people unable to save themselves.
A provision established by God.
A lifted sign.
And life offered to those who responded to God's promise.
Then look toward Golgotha.
A world ruined by sin.
Humanity unable to earn its own redemption.
The Son sent by the Father.
A Savior lifted upon a Roman cross.
And eternal life promised to everyone who believes in Him.
Do you see why Jesus chose that story?
He was preparing Nicodemus to understand that the Messiah had come not merely to teach humanity how to behave.
He had come to save.
And then Jesus spoke the words that have traveled across centuries, continents, languages, prison cells, hospital rooms, funeral services, childhood memories, and countless broken hearts.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” — John 3:16, KJV
But there is something important in the original Greek that deserves our attention.
The verse begins:
Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον
Houtōs gar ēgapēsen ho theos ton kosmon.
“For God loved the world in this way…”
The Greek οὕτως (houtōs) emphasizes the manner in which God's love was demonstrated.
The familiar translation “God so loved the world” is not wrong, but the expression is not merely telling us that God loved the world very much.
It is showing us how God demonstrated His love.
He gave His Son.
God's love was not left as an invisible sentiment.
It entered human history.
It took on flesh.
It walked among sinners.
It touched lepers.
It welcomed the repentant.
It confronted hypocrisy.
It wept at a tomb.
And ultimately, the Son willingly laid down His life.
This is why John 3:16 cannot be separated from John 3:14.
The love of God is revealed through the giving of the Son who would be lifted up.
The Cross was not an emergency response to a plan that had failed.
It was central to God's saving purpose.
And perhaps the most astonishing part is the kind of world God loved.
The Greek word κόσμος (kosmos) is used here for the world of humanity.
Not a world that had finally made itself worthy.
Not a world that had repented perfectly.
Not a world that had learned how to stop rebelling.
A world that needed saving.
Romans 5:8 puts it this way:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we finally conquered every temptation.
Not after we became people whose past no longer embarrassed us.
While we were still sinners.
That does not mean sin is harmless.
It means God's grace is astonishing.
It means the Savior did not wait until the wounded became healthy enough to deserve a physician.
He came because they needed one.
And this is where the wilderness story begins to sound painfully familiar.
Maybe your wilderness is not filled with visible serpents.
Maybe it is filled with things nobody sees.
A marriage that has become cold.
A secret addiction you keep promising to abandon.
A bitterness you have carried for years.
A betrayal you still cannot forgive.
A habit of lying because you are terrified of being exposed.
A prayer life that slowly disappeared.
A Bible collecting dust beside a phone that receives hours of your attention.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe people still come to you for spiritual advice.
And maybe, somewhere beneath the appearance of strength, you know something is wrong.
You have learned how to appear spiritually alive while privately feeling distant from God.
Nicodemus knew what it meant to be respected.
The Israelites knew what it meant to have witnessed miracles.
Neither religious knowledge nor past spiritual experiences could replace their present need for God's mercy.
And neither can yours.
You can grow up in a Christian home and still need to be born from above.
You can know every word of John 3:16 and still need to personally trust the Christ it proclaims.
You can own a hundred Bibles and still refuse to listen when God confronts your heart.
You can sing about surrender while holding tightly to the very sin that is destroying your peace.
And yet the invitation of Jesus remains.
Come into the light.
John 3 does not end with the declaration that God loves the world.
It continues with a confrontation about why people resist the light.
“And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.” — John 3:19, KJV
That verse is difficult because it exposes something deeper than ignorance.
Sometimes we do not avoid God because we do not know what He wants.
Sometimes we avoid Him because we do.
We know the relationship needs to end.
We know the apology needs to be made.
We know the dishonesty needs to stop.
We know the hidden habit is becoming a master.
We know that the bitterness we keep feeding is poisoning our own hearts.
But darkness feels safer because it allows us to maintain the illusion of control.
Until the darkness begins taking more than it promised.
And that is why the Gospel is both comforting and confronting.
Jesus does not offer salvation by pretending our sin is insignificant.
He offers salvation because our sin is serious enough that we needed a Redeemer.
The Cross tells us two truths at once.
Our sin is more terrible than we wanted to admit.
And God's love in Christ is more extraordinary than we dared to imagine.
Consider the people bitten in the wilderness.
The text does not describe a lengthy process of moral rehabilitation before they could receive God's promised healing.
They were commanded to look toward the provision God had established.
Their deliverance did not arise from the excellence of their own efforts.
It came from the mercy of God.
In the same way, eternal life is not something we purchase through religious performance.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast.
Yet saving faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting Him as the Savior and Lord He truly is.
And genuine faith does not make repentance unnecessary.
It brings us toward the light.
Repentance is not a payment we make to convince God to love us.
It is the turning of a heart that recognizes its sin and comes to Christ for mercy.
Grace does not give us permission to cherish the poison.
Grace calls us out of the life that was destroying us.
Perhaps that is what somebody reading this needs to hear.
You do not have to keep defending the sin that Jesus is calling you to confess.
You do not have to pretend your wounds are healed.
You do not have to manufacture a spotless history before approaching the Savior.
But neither should you confuse His patience with permission to remain unchanged.
Come to Him.
Not with a performance.
Not with another excuse.
With the truth.
“Lord, I have sinned.”
“Lord, I have wandered.”
“Lord, I have been hiding.”
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
Those are not the words of someone who has everything figured out.
They are the words of someone beginning to recognize where help must come from.
And if that is where you are today, do not underestimate the significance of turning toward Christ.
The same Gospel that exposes sin also announces forgiveness.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The promise is grounded in God's faithfulness and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Not in our ability to cry convincingly.
Not in how many people approve of our testimony.
Not in how perfectly we describe our remorse.
In Him.
And there is another detail about John 3 that I cannot stop thinking about.
Nicodemus came to Jesus at night.
John does not explicitly tell us every reason he chose that hour, so we should not pretend to know all his motives.
But the setting becomes striking when read alongside the chapter's language of darkness and light.
A respected teacher came with questions.
Jesus answered with the necessity of new birth and the promise of eternal life.
Later, Nicodemus appears again in John 7:50–52, raising a question about whether Jesus should be judged without a proper hearing.
Then, after the crucifixion, he appears in John 19:39, bringing a substantial mixture of myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial.
The Gospel does not give us a complete account of Nicodemus's inner spiritual journey, and we should not invent one.
But it does allow us to see a man who first approached Jesus at night later participating in the burial of the crucified Lord.
The teacher who heard about the Son of Man being lifted up eventually stood in the aftermath of that lifting up.
What must he have remembered?
Did the words from that nighttime conversation return to him?
Did he think about Moses?
The serpent?
The promise?
We are not told.
But the question lingers.
Because what Jesus had spoken about was no longer merely a mysterious future event.
The Son of Man had been lifted up.
The Cross had happened.
And the story did not end at the tomb.
Jesus rose from the dead.
That is the glory of the Gospel.
The One who died for sins was raised.
The crucified Savior is the risen Lord.
His resurrection is not an optional decoration added to the Christian message.
It is central to the good news we proclaim.
As Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 15, Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures.
The bronze serpent could not rise.
It was metal.
It could not speak.
It could not love.
It could not intercede.
But Jesus lives.
And because He lives, the invitation of John 3:16 is not merely a memory of something God once offered.
It is a living call to trust the risen Christ.
Now perhaps you understand why the words “whosoever believeth in him” are so precious.
The invitation is not restricted to people with respectable histories.
It is not reserved for those who have never fallen.
It is not limited to those who already understand every doctrine or have solved every question.
The promise is for everyone who truly believes in the Son.
That includes the ashamed.
The religiously exhausted.
The person who once mocked Christianity.
The believer who has wandered and needs to return.
The person who has spent years trying to outrun a guilty conscience.
The person who wonders whether anyone could still love them if the truth were known.
The Gospel does not say your past was harmless.
It says Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
And that is the heart of our message:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because consequences always disappear.
But because the grace of Christ can transform the story of a sinner who comes to Him.
A thief dying beside Jesus heard the promise of paradise.
A persecutor named Saul became a witness to the Christ he once opposed.
Peter, who denied his Lord, was restored and commissioned to care for His sheep.
Their sins were not celebrated.
Their Savior was.
That is what redemption does.
It does not turn darkness into something good by renaming it.
It reveals the power of God to rescue people from darkness and bring them into His marvelous light.
And perhaps your story is not finished either.
Maybe there are chapters you wish you could erase.
Things you said.
People you hurt.
Choices that cost more than you imagined.
Years you cannot recover.
Maybe you have been telling yourself that God can use other people, but not someone with your history.
But listen carefully.
The Cross does not promise that every earthly consequence will vanish.
It does promise that forgiveness and new life are found in Jesus Christ.
And the Lord who calls you to repentance is also the Lord who welcomes sinners who come to Him.
You are not being invited to worship your past.
You are being invited to follow your Savior.
And if you have been running from Him, this may be the moment to stop.
Not because an article has the power to save you.
None of them can.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
But God's Word calls us to respond to the truth.
And perhaps today you are finally ready to be honest.
You do not have to reveal private details or confess your deepest wounds publicly. God knows what you are carrying even when other people do not.
Your story may remind another struggling person that returning to Jesus is still possible.
There is someone in your circle who may need this message.
Perhaps a brother who has stopped attending church.
A sister who smiles in public but cries when she is alone.
A friend who believes they have sinned too much to come back.
A parent praying for a wandering child.
A young believer struggling to understand why Jesus had to die.
Or someone who has never understood that John 3:16 is not simply a beautiful slogan, but a declaration of God's saving love through the crucified and risen Son.
Not as a performance of spirituality, but as a way of placing the message of Christ where someone else might encounter it.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build a community around personalities.
It is to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
And if these writings have helped you understand Scripture more deeply, return to prayer, confront sin, or rediscover the beauty of the Gospel, I want to extend a personal invitation.

Scripture teaches the importance of generous support for Gospel ministry. In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul reminds believers that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
You are not buying God's favor.
You are not purchasing forgiveness.
You are not earning a higher place in heaven.
You are simply choosing to help make Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
And that partnership matters.
Every article requires care.
Every Scripture explanation should be handled responsibly.
Every resource prepared for struggling believers, new Christians, and serious students of the Bible represents an opportunity to serve.
But the greatest reason to partner is not merchandise.
It is the mission.
To help people open their Bibles.
To encourage weary believers.
To call wandering hearts back to Christ.
To remind sinners that repentance and forgiveness are not outdated religious ideas, but essential truths of the Gospel.
To keep telling the story of the Savior who was lifted up so that those who believe in Him might have eternal life.
Use those resources.
Study the Scriptures.
Test what you read against God's Word.
Grow in prayer.
Stay connected to a faithful local church.
Learn to recognize the difference between biblical truth and religious-sounding promises that Scripture never made.
And remember that even a simple act of sharing an article can help someone encounter a passage of Scripture they may otherwise never have considered.
Sharing, praying, encouraging others, and faithfully living out the Gospel are meaningful ways to participate too.
But before you leave, I want to return to the wilderness one final time.
Imagine a wounded Israelite.
The bite has already happened.
The venom is doing its terrible work.
The person cannot undo the bite.
Cannot reverse the moment.
Cannot negotiate with the consequences.
But somewhere in the camp, Moses has raised the bronze serpent in obedience to God's command.
And the word has gone out.
Look.
The promise is not that the bite never occurred.
The promise is that God has provided a way for the bitten to live.
Now look toward Calvary.
The Son of God has been lifted up.
He has borne sin.
He has died.
He has risen.
And the Gospel announces that everyone who believes in Him will not perish but have eternal life.
Perhaps you have spent years looking everywhere else.
Looking toward achievement to quiet your guilt.
Looking toward religion to prove you are good enough.
Looking toward entertainment to silence your conscience.
Looking toward other people's approval to convince yourself that you are worth something.
Looking toward tomorrow because you keep telling yourself that someday you will finally surrender.
But salvation is not found in another version of yourself.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking tragedy would be to spend your whole life knowing the words of John 3:16 without ever coming to the Savior those words reveal.
So read the verse again.
Slowly.
“For God so loved the world…”
That includes a world filled with people who have rebelled against Him.
“That he gave his only begotten Son…”
The Father's love revealed through the gift of His unique and beloved Son.
“That whosoever believeth in him…”
An invitation to genuine faith in Christ.
“Should not perish…”
Rescue from the judgment our sins deserve.
“But have everlasting life.”
Life in fellowship with God, secured through the crucified and risen Savior.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we were good enough to climb up to heaven.
But that God, in His mercy, sent His Son to save sinners.
Not that sin was too small to matter.
But that Jesus Christ was willing and able to bear its cost.
Not that grace leaves us unchanged.
But that the One who saves also calls us into a new life of repentance, faith, and obedience.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, do not mistake admiration for surrender.
Turn to Him.
Believe His Gospel.
Ask Him for mercy.
And if you already belong to Christ but have wandered, do not use your failures as an excuse to remain far away.
Confess your sins.
Return to His Word.
Seek the help of mature believers where you need it.
Keep walking with the Savior who is faithful.
Because the story of the bronze serpent was never meant to leave us staring at a piece of metal in the desert.
It was meant, through the words of Jesus Himself, to direct our attention to something infinitely greater.
A Savior lifted up.
A love demonstrated.
A sacrifice accomplished.
A tomb left empty.
And eternal life offered through faith in the Son of God.
So when you hear John 3:16 again, remember what came before it.
Remember the wilderness.
Remember the wounded.
Remember the mercy of God.
And above all, remember Jesus.
One final thought.
The people in the wilderness could not go backward and undo the bite.
But by God's mercy, they could look toward the provision He had made.
You cannot go backward and rewrite yesterday either.
But in Jesus Christ, forgiveness is real, redemption is possible, and a new life can begin.
The wound may be part of your history, but through Jesus Christ, it does not have to be the final word of your story.
